title: Vagal Sensory Neurons: The Body Reports to the Brain

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: An {{c1::afferent}} carries sensory signals from the body toward the central nervous system.
cards.quote: An afferent is a sensory fibre that carries signals from the body toward the central nervous system.

cards.front: What does interoception sense?
cards.back: The body's internal state, such as lung volume, blood pressure and gut fullness.
cards.quote: Interoception is the sense of the body's own internal state: lung volume, blood pressure, how full the gut is.

cards.front: Which three questions require separate evidence when characterizing a vagal sensory population?
cards.back: What stimulus activates it? What channel converts that stimulus into current? What output changes when the cells are driven or removed?
cards.quote: Each needs its own evidence, and evidence for one does not by itself answer the others.

cards.front: Why does a receptor-based genetic label alone fail to identify what a sensory population detects?
cards.back: It provides access to labelled cells; it does not establish their natural stimulus, the receptor’s causal role in transduction, or their output.
cards.quote: but labelling alone establishes neither the natural stimulus, nor the protein's causal role in transduction, nor the output.

cards.front: Driving a sensory population and producing an output tests {{c1::sufficiency}} for that output.
cards.back: The conclusion applies to the tested conditions.
cards.quote: Driving a population and seeing an output appear is a test of sufficiency: these cells can produce it.

cards.front: Activating a labelled sensory population changes breathing in anaesthetized mice. What intervention would test whether it is necessary for a naturally evoked breathing response?
cards.back: Silence or remove the population, apply the natural stimulus, and test whether the response fails. Necessity would be limited to that assay, age and driver.
cards.quote: Removing or silencing the population and seeing the output fail is a test of necessity: in that assay, at that age, with that driver.

cards.front: Why do the GPR65-labelled vagal findings fail to establish a single food-to-satiety pathway?
cards.back: They respond to intestinal food and can suppress gastric contractions under anaesthesia, but activation did not measurably change feeding in the tested awake-mouse assays.
cards.quote: Responding to a nutrient, controlling the stomach and ending a meal are three different measurements,
cards.section: One worked case, because it is the cleanest

cards.front: Where are vagal sensory neuron cell bodies located near the base of the skull?
cards.back: In the nodose and jugular ganglia.
cards.quote: Vagal sensory cell bodies sit in two ganglia at the base of the skull, the nodose and the jugular,
cards.section: One nerve, many labelled lines: genetic access to vagal afferents

cards.front: What breathing patterns followed light activation of P2ry1-labelled versus Npy2r-labelled vagal neurons in deeply anaesthetized mice?
cards.back: P2ry1 activation suppressed breathing; Npy2r activation produced rapid shallow breathing.
cards.quote: P2ry1 activation suppressed breathing. Npy2r activation produced rapid shallow breathing.
cards.section: One nerve, many labelled lines: genetic access to vagal afferents

cards.front: How do myelination and conduction speed distinguish A fibres from C fibres?
cards.back: A fibres are myelinated and conduct quickly; C fibres are unmyelinated and conduct slowly.
cards.quote: fast A fibres, which are myelinated and conduct quickly,
cards.section: One nerve, many labelled lines: genetic access to vagal afferents

cards.front: Two labelled sensory populations conduct predominantly at different speeds. Does that establish completely non-overlapping populations or their natural stimuli?
cards.back: Neither. Different predominant conduction classes support physiological differences, but allow overlap and do not identify natural stimuli.
cards.quote: It is not proof that the two sets are wholly separate, and it says nothing about what stimulus drives either in life:
cards.section: One nerve, many labelled lines: genetic access to vagal afferents

cards.front: In mouse gut imaging using a reporter carried from development, what stimulated GLP1R-labelled vagal neurons?
cards.back: Stretch of the stomach and intestine; the intestinal finding remains reporter-dependent and unresolved for this line.
cards.quote: GLP1R-labelled neurons responded to stretch of the stomach and intestine.
cards.section: One nerve, many labelled lines: genetic access to vagal afferents

cards.front: Developmental-reporter imaging finds intestinal stretch responses in GLP1R-labelled mouse neurons, but adult viral labelling finds no intestinal stretch endings. How should the results be reconciled?
cards.back: The imaging identifies responses in its labelled cells; the anatomy identifies endings reached by the adult tool. Gastric stretch afferents are supported across preparations. Intestinal stretch remains reporter-dependent and unresolved. The rule is that a genetic handle depends on both driver and tool.
cards.quote: Carry forward that the labelled cells include gastric stretch afferents, and treat the intestinal stretch finding as reporter-dependent and unresolved for this line.
cards.section: One nerve, many labelled lines: genetic access to vagal afferents

cards.front: The {{c1::Hering-Breuer inflation reflex}} cuts short further inspiration as the lungs fill.
cards.back: Its stimulus is lung stretch.
cards.quote: When the lungs fill, further inspiration is cut short.
cards.section: Two different populations, one outcome: breathing stops

cards.front: Why does halted inspiration alone fail to distinguish airway protection from lung inflation sensing?
cards.back: Both can halt inspiration, but protection is evoked by laryngeal irritants such as water or acid, whereas inflation sensing reports stretch.
cards.quote: the same output can be reached from two different stimuli through two different populations,
cards.section: Two different populations, one outcome: breathing stops

cards.front: What does impaired water- and acid-evoked swallowing after P2ry1-cell ablation establish in mice?
cards.back: Those cells are needed for the tested swallowing response. It does not establish direct water or acid transduction or necessity for every protective response.
cards.quote: They then ablated the P2ry1 cells genetically, and swallowing evoked by water and acid at the larynx was impaired.
cards.section: Two different populations, one outcome: breathing stops

cards.front: In mouse ganglion imaging, most inflation-responsive cells are PIEZO2-positive and P2RY1-negative. What happens to the claim that P2ry1 airway-defence cells also account for inflation sensing, and why?
cards.back: The claim is undermined: most inflation-responsive cells belong to the other labelled population, so a shared breathing output does not establish a shared sensory pathway.
cards.quote: Most stretch-responsive neurons were PIEZO2-positive and P2RY1-negative — the other population.
cards.section: Two different populations, one outcome: breathing stops

cards.front: Why does loss of a reflex after sensory-neuron channel deletion not by itself prove that the channel directly converts force into current?
cards.back: Deletion shows requirement in targeted cells. Direct force transduction also needs mechanosensitive-current recordings and evidence that force gates the channel itself.
cards.quote: Showing that the same protein is the thing that converts force into current also takes recordings of mechanosensitive current
cards.section: What transduces force in the lung and the artery

cards.front: Piezo2 is conditionally deleted in adult mouse sensory neurons. What happens to the lung inflation reflex, and what does this show?
cards.back: The inflation reflex is impaired, supporting a requirement for Piezo2 in the targeted adult sensory neurons. This is distinct from activating Piezo2-labelled neurons or deleting Piezo2 during development.
cards.quote: deleted Piezo2 conditionally in sensory neurons of adult mice, which impaired the inflation reflex.
cards.section: What transduces force in the lung and the artery

cards.front: What heart-rate response defines the arterial baroreflex when blood pressure rises?
cards.back: Heart rate slows.
cards.quote: The baroreflex is the reflex by which a rise in blood pressure slows the heart;
cards.section: What transduces force in the lung and the artery

cards.front: What does the mouse baroreflex deletion experiment establish about Piezo1 and Piezo2 in targeted nodose and petrosal neurons?
cards.back: They are required collectively: either single deletion caused no detectable reflex change against controls, while deleting both abolished the reflex.
cards.quote: a collective requirement for Piezo1 and Piezo2.
cards.section: What transduces force in the lung and the artery

cards.front: Piezo1/Piezo2 double deletion abolishes a mouse baroreflex, while single deletions show no detectable population effect. Design a test distinguishing both channels in each baroreceptor from separate single-channel populations.
cards.back: Identify baroreceptors, measure channel expression cell by cell, and test validated single-channel deletions under controlled mechanical stimulation. The rule is that population reflex output neither assigns channels to individual cells nor quantifies the input lost.
cards.quote: Separating the pictures would mean identifying baroreceptors and testing, cell by cell, which channels they express and which they need
cards.section: What transduces force in the lung and the artery

cards.front: Vagal sensory axons primarily target the {{c1::nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS)}} in the medulla.
cards.back: This relay distributes visceral input to circuits controlling breathing, circulation and digestion.
cards.quote: Vagal sensory axons primarily target the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) in the medulla,
cards.section: A map of the organs in the brainstem, sharpened by inhibition

cards.front: Organ-responsive brainstem neurons receive local inhibitory input. If this inhibition keeps organ responses separate, what should blocking it do to organ tuning, and why?
cards.back: Tuning should broaden across organs because previously suppressed responses can emerge. This supports active sharpening of the map by inhibition.
cards.quote: So the separation depends on inhibition rather than on anatomy alone.
cards.section: A map of the organs in the brainstem, sharpened by inhibition

cards.front: In anaesthetized mouse NTS imaging, cutting both vagi below the diaphragm removes the gastric-distension response. What does this establish?
cards.back: The response depends on the subdiaphragmatic vagal route. It does not identify which peripheral transduction channel generated the signal.
cards.quote: Cutting the vagus below the diaphragm on both sides removed the gastric distension response, which confirmed the route.
cards.section: A map of the organs in the brainstem, sharpened by inhibition

cards.front: Why are intestinal afferent endings near myenteric ganglia compatible with tension sensing without proving it?
cards.back: Their location fits gut-wall tension detection, but anatomy alone does not establish a response to mechanical stimulation.
cards.quote: That location is compatible with sensing gut-wall tension; anatomy alone neither establishes mechanosensitivity nor requires every stretch detector to sit there.
cards.section: From afferent to behaviour: stretch, satiety and what the trial evidence covers

cards.front: How did activation of Oxtr-positive intestinal stretch afferents compare with Glp1r-positive afferents in awake-mouse feeding assays?
cards.back: Oxtr-positive activation strongly suppressed feeding; Glp1r-positive activation suppressed it more weakly.
cards.quote: Activating Oxtr-positive intestinal stretch afferents strongly suppressed feeding;
cards.section: From afferent to behaviour: stretch, satiety and what the trial evidence covers

cards.front: Why does reduced intake after a non-nutritive hyperosmolar intestinal load show nutrient independence without isolating volume as the cause?
cards.back: Nutrients are absent, but the load also draws fluid into the gut. Osmolality must be matched and resulting distension measured to credit volume itself.
cards.quote: The load was not a pure volume change either: a hyperosmolar load pulls fluid into the gut.
cards.section: From afferent to behaviour: stretch, satiety and what the trial evidence covers

cards.front: A nutrient triggers hormone release from gut epithelial cells, and that hormone acts on a vagal terminal. What does a resulting afferent response imply about direct nutrient sensing, and why?
cards.back: Direct nutrient sensing by the afferent is not established: the hormone can relay the nutrient signal from the epithelial cell.
cards.quote: So a nutrient signal could reach an afferent without that afferent sensing the nutrient itself
cards.section: From afferent to behaviour: stretch, satiety and what the trial evidence covers

cards.front: Design an awake-mouse intake experiment that separates a gut-volume signal from nutrient content while allowing an indirect hormone route to vagal afferents.
cards.back: Compare equal-volume nutrient and non-nutritive loads with matched osmolality and measured distension. Measure intake and add a vagal route control. The rules are to dissociate stimuli and allow epithelial hormone signalling; equal delivered volume alone does not control osmotic fluid shifts.
cards.quote: Crediting volume itself would need osmolality-matched loads and measured distension, because of the osmotic fluid shift.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Activating a stretch-afferent population reduces mouse intake. If reversible silencing instead increases intake during a large meal, what follows, and why?
cards.back: The population is needed to limit intake in that large-meal assay. Silencing supplies necessity evidence that the activation result alone could not provide.
cards.quote: If silencing the stretch population raises intake of a large meal, that population is needed there.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why can the implanted VNS-REHAB stroke trial not identify the vagal sensory population or transduction mechanism responsible for its motor benefit?
cards.back: No selected population was labelled. Its evidence concerns an implanted device paired with rehabilitation, not a natural stimulus or a cell-specific mechanism.
cards.quote: because no population is labelled. It covers one device and one pairing with rehabilitation,
cards.section: From afferent to behaviour: stretch, satiety and what the trial evidence covers

cards.front: What are the embryonic origins of nodose and jugular sensory neurons?
cards.back: Nodose neurons derive from epibranchial placodes; jugular neurons derive from neural crest.
cards.quote: nodose neurons derive from epibranchial placodes (thickenings of embryonic head ectoderm), and jugular neurons from neural crest.
cards.section: Ganglia, atlases and the 18 versus 37 counts

cards.front: Why should atlas counts of 18 nodose types and 37 combined vagal/glossopharyngeal types not be treated as conflicting counts of the same population?
cards.back: The sampled populations differ in scope. Transcriptomic types also remain functional hypotheses unless physiology or behaviour establishes their roles.
cards.quote: The two counts differ in scope and are not interchangeable.
cards.section: Ganglia, atlases and the 18 versus 37 counts

cards.front: P2ry1-cell ablation and P2X2/P2X3 receptor loss both impair mouse laryngeal swallowing. Must these be parallel pathways? Give a compatible alternative.
cards.back: No. Epithelial detection could lead to ATP signalling through P2X2/P2X3 onto P2ry1-labelled afferents in one serial pathway. The rule is that requiring both components does not establish separate routes; these interventions do not prove that serial arrangement either.
cards.quote: Requiring both the cells and the receptors is compatible with one serial pathway,
cards.section: Before the nerve: an epithelial step and a candidate cell type

cards.front: In mice, pulmonary neuroendocrine cells express Piezo2, but the inflation-reflex defect follows deletion in adult sensory neurons. Which cell-level causal assignment is supported, and why?
cards.back: The loss-of-function evidence supports a neuronal Piezo2 requirement, not a requirement in the neuroendocrine cells. The rule is that expression alone cannot assign a reflex to a cell type; the targeted deletion determines the causal scope.
cards.quote: so epithelial expression on its own does not assign the reflex to the neuroendocrine cells.
cards.section: Before the nerve: an epithelial step and a candidate cell type

cards.front: A mouse cell expressed a Cre driver only during development. What labelling difference is expected between a permanent developmental reporter and a Cre-dependent virus delivered in adulthood, and why?
cards.back: The developmental reporter can retain a label from past Cre activity; the adult virus may miss that cell because it mainly captures activity after arrival. Labelling efficiency and specificity still require validation.
cards.quote: can mark cells by their past driver activity.
cards.section: Why the Glp1r-Cre line changed its answer

cards.front: In mice, early broad Piezo2 deletion causes newborn respiratory distress and death, but nodose-only deletion leaves pups alive with normal blood oxygen. Does this assign the deaths to nodose Piezo2 loss?
cards.back: No. The nodose-only deletion did not reproduce the lethal phenotype. The neonatal broad-deletion result also cannot substitute for the separate adult inflation-reflex experiment.
cards.quote: those pups survived with normal blood oxygen, so the neonatal deaths were not caused by loss in the airway-innervating nodose population.
cards.section: Piezo2 in newborns and the baroreflex numbers

cards.front: In a hypothetical baroreflex measurement, sensitivity is constant at -5.0 bpm/mmHg while pressure rises by 10 mmHg. What heart-rate change does this predict?
cards.back: ΔHR = sensitivity × Δpressure = (-5.0 bpm/mmHg) × 10 mmHg = -50 bpm: a fall of 50 bpm.
cards.quote: its sensitivity is the change in heart rate per unit rise in pressure, in beats per minute per mmHg.
cards.section: What transduces force in the lung and the artery

cards.front: For the illustrative model F(x) = 5 × (1 + 0.35²) × x² / (0.35² + x²), with F in bpm/mmHg, calculate F(0.5) and its drop from F(1).
cards.back: F(1) = 5.00 bpm/mmHg. F(0.5) = 5 × 1.1225 × 0.25 / 0.3725 ≈ 3.77 bpm/mmHg; the magnitude drops by about 1.23 bpm/mmHg. These are model predictions, not measured single-deletion effects.
cards.quote: where x is a hypothetical fraction of control sensory input and F is the predicted magnitude of baroreflex sensitivity in bpm/mmHg.
cards.section: Worked problem: one way a single deletion could stay invisible

cards.front: Two hypothetical independent groups each have a baroreflex-sensitivity SEM of 0.5 bpm/mmHg. Calculate the SEM of their difference and an approximate two-SEM cutoff.
cards.back: SEMdifference = √(0.5² + 0.5²) ≈ 0.71 bpm/mmHg. Two SEM ≈ 1.41 bpm/mmHg. This illustrates error-bar arithmetic; it is not the published single-deletion experiment’s detection limit.
cards.quote: The single-deletion groups' own standard errors, sample sizes, test and power are not given here,
cards.section: Worked problem: one way a single deletion could stay invisible

cards.front: A chosen saturating input-to-reflex model predicts that half-input loss falls below an illustrative cutoff. Why does this fail to prove that a single channel deletion must be missed?
cards.back: The half-input effect depends on where the assumed curve bends; other saturating curves give larger drops. Sampling can also move an estimate across the cutoff. The rules are that the curve and input loss were unmeasured choices, and an illustrative cutoff does not establish actual experimental power.
cards.quote: Saturation on its own tells you nothing about the half-input effect, because the answer depends on where the curve bends.
cards.section: Worked problem: one way a single deletion could stay invisible

cards.front: In a hypothetical organ-response imaging panel in anaesthetized mice, 750 neurons respond and 600 respond to only one tested organ. What percentage responds to multiple organs, and what is its denominator?
cards.back: Multi-organ count = 750 − 600 = 150; percentage = 100 × 150/750 = 20%. The denominator is the 750 neurons responsive to this panel in this preparation.
cards.quote: The denominator is neurons responsive to this panel in an anaesthetized mouse, not all NTS neurons and not awake humans.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading the NTS map

cards.front: An organ-response imaging study pools neurons from six mice. Why would treating every recorded neuron as an independent animal overstate the replication?
cards.back: Neurons are nested within mice, so the cell count is not the number of independent animals. The rule is to distinguish the counted response units from independent biological replication when interpreting organ-selectivity estimates.
cards.quote: The 1,133 cells come from six mice, so they are not 1,133 independent units.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading the NTS map

cards.front: In a mouse NTS data set, 42.2% of glucose-responsive cells also respond to duodenal distension, while 31.0% of distension-responsive cells respond to glucose. What is the distension/glucose population-size ratio?
cards.back: Let overlap be I, glucose cells G and distension cells S. I = 0.422G = 0.310S, so S/G = 0.422/0.310 ≈ 1.36. The distension-responsive population is about 36% larger; published rounding makes this approximate.
cards.quote: The two percentages are consistent: the stretch-responsive population is about 36 percent larger, which gives the smaller conditional fraction.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading the NTS map
